bug_description.normalized: Stage 01 reproduced AddressSanitizer double-free in mruby. The staged text witness is converted by `proto_to_ruby.cpp` into Ruby whose relevant fragment is `[1, 0].insert((((1 >> ((1 - (7)) * (10))) >> 1) - (1 - ((9) >> ((1 - (11)) - (11))))))`. Under mruby's integer shift semantics, the negative shift counts make that expression evaluate to the single huge positive index `576460752322297855`, and the call passes no inserted objects, so `Array#insert` forwards `self[idx, 0] = []` into `mrb_ary_splice`. The literal `[1, 0]` is heap-backed, `mrb_ary_splice` asks `ary_expand_capa` to grow it to `head + argc = 576460752322297855`, and `ary_expand_capa` therefore requests `sizeof(mrb_value) * capa = 0x8000000011fffff0` bytes; the saved ASan run prints two failed allocations of that exact size. Vulnerable `mrb_realloc` then frees the original array buffer when `realloc` returns NULL and raises NoMemoryError before `ary_expand_capa` can install a replacement pointer. The array object keeps the freed buffer in `a->as.heap.ptr`, and `mrb_close -> mrb_gc_destroy -> obj_free` frees that same pointer again during teardown. The fixing commit removes the failure-path `mrb_free(mrb, p)` from `mrb_realloc`.

source.description: First project statement that turns the witness-derived giant insert index into the oversized splice request. `Array#insert` forwards the attacker-controlled `idx` and the empty varargs array into `[]=`.
source.value_from: The staged `poc` text plus `oss-fuzz/proto_to_ruby.cpp` deterministically emit the relevant Ruby call `[1, (0)].insert((((1 >> ((1 - (7)) * (10))) >> 1) - (1 - ((9) >> ((1 - (11)) - (11))))))`. In mruby, negative right-shift counts are redirected to left shifts, so this evaluates to `idx = 576460752322297855`; because the call supplies no additional insert arguments, `args` is `[]`.
source.note: This is the first project-code statement that materializes the attacker-controlled arithmetic result as array-growth state. `idx < 0` at line 575 is false for this witness, so the giant positive index reaches `[]=` unchanged.

tainted_value_origin.description: The generated literal `[1, 0]` allocates a heap-backed element buffer. This exact pointer is later passed into `mrb_realloc`, freed on the OOM path, and freed again during GC teardown.
tainted_value_origin.value_from: The relevant generated Ruby fragment starts with the literal receiver `[1, (0)]`. Its size is two elements, so `ary_new_capa` allocates heap storage instead of using the embedded-array path.
tainted_value_origin.note: ASan's allocation stack names `ary_new_capa` line 37 under `mrb_malloc`, matching this buffer allocation.

sink.description: Second free. During `mrb_close` teardown, `obj_free` sees the array is heap-backed and calls `mrb_free` on the stale `a->as.heap.ptr` left behind by the failed reallocation path.
sink.note: The saved sanitizer trace reports the crashing free through `mrb_default_allocf -> mrb_free -> obj_free`; line 855 is the array-specific source-level free site inside `obj_free`.

root_cause.description: Failure-path ownership bug. When `realloc` returns NULL for a nonzero length, vulnerable `mrb_realloc` frees the still-owned original buffer before raising NoMemoryError, even though callers like `ary_expand_capa` still expect `p` to remain valid on allocation failure.
root_cause.note: The fixing commit deletes this line and instead only raises the no-memory exception. That preserves the original array buffer until normal cleanup and removes the double-free.

parser_admitted.description: The generated Ruby parses and codegens successfully, so execution enters the VM and reaches the `Array#insert` / `mrb_ary_aset` path seen in the saved ASan stacks.
parser_admitted.note: The crash trace later passes through `mrb_vm_exec -> mrb_ary_aset -> mrb_ary_splice`, which confirms the script was admitted and executed rather than failing during parsing.

coarse_trace.summary: The staged text witness is deterministically converted into Ruby that builds the literal receiver `[1, 0]` and calls `.insert(...)` with a single huge positive index expression.
mruby allocates a heap-backed buffer for the two-element literal array, then `Array#insert` forwards the witness-derived index `576460752322297855` and the empty payload `[]` into `[]=`.

`mrb_ary_aset` materializes `head = 576460752322297855`, `len = 0`, and `rpl = []`; `mrb_ary_splice` derives `head + argc` as the new length and asks `ary_expand_capa` to realloc the original array buffer to that enormous capacity.

The `0x8000000011fffff0`-byte realloc request fails, and vulnerable `mrb_realloc` frees the original buffer before raising NoMemoryError, so `ary_expand_capa` unwinds without installing a replacement pointer.
Later `mrb_close` teardown frees the same heap pointer again from the array object, and ASan reports the second free via `obj_free -> mrb_free -> mrb_default_allocf`.

fine_trace.note: The staged `poc` file is plain text for the `ruby_fuzzer::Function` message, not opaque binary. Visiting that message deterministically emits the relevant Ruby fragment `[1, (0)].insert((((1 >> ((1 - (7)) * (10))) >> 1) - (1 - ((9) >> ((1 - (11)) - (11))))))`: `visit(Const)` reduces each integer literal modulo 13, empty constants become `1`, and the array builtin prints `.insert(...)` on the literal receiver.

Before calling `insert`, the generated literal receiver `[1, 0]` is materialized as an `RArray`. Because the literal has two elements, this path allocates heap storage for those elements and stores the resulting pointer in `a->as.heap.ptr`; ASan's allocation stack records this same line under `mrb_malloc`.

Source. The witness-generated call passes no extra objects, so `args` is `[]`. The index expression evaluates to `576460752322297855`: `1 >> -60` is redirected to `1 << 60` by mruby's integer shift implementation, the remaining arithmetic yields `-18874367` on the right-hand side, and the final subtraction stays below `ARY_MAX_SIZE`. Because `idx` is positive, line 575 does not adjust it and this line forwards the giant index unchanged into `[]=`.

fine_trace.code: mrb_ary_splice(mrb, self, aget_index(mrb, v1), aget_index(mrb, v2), v3);
fine_trace.note: The three-argument `[]=` call materializes the splice parameters in C: `aget_index(v1)` converts the Ruby `idx` to `head = 576460752322297855`, `aget_index(v2)` gives replacement length `0`, and `v3` is the empty replacement array `[]`.

Here `rpl` is the empty array from step 4, so `argc = 0`. The receiver array length `alen` is only 2, so the `head >= alen` branch is taken. `head` is still below `ARY_MAX_SIZE`, so no `IndexError` is raised; instead `len` becomes `head + argc = 576460752322297855`, and `ary_expand_capa` is called because that length exceeds the current capacity of the two-element array.

The growth request is made against the original heap buffer from step 2. With `capa = 576460752322297855`, this asks for `sizeof(mrb_value) * capa = 0x8000000011fffff0` bytes; the saved ASan trace prints two warnings that allocation of exactly `0x8000000011fffff0` bytes failed, so this call enters `mrb_realloc`'s NULL-result path.

Root cause. `mrb_realloc_simple` has already returned `NULL` for the huge nonzero request from step 6, but vulnerable `mrb_realloc` frees the still-owned original buffer `p` before setting `out_of_memory` and raising NoMemoryError. The patch removes this free so callers keep ownership of `p` on allocation failure.

These state updates are never reached on the failing path, because step 7 raises NoMemoryError after freeing the old buffer. `ary_expand_capa` therefore unwinds while the array object still carries the step-2 pointer in `a->as.heap.ptr`, even though that pointer has already been freed.

Sink. `FuzzRB` always calls `mrb_close(mrb)`, and `mrb_gc_destroy` teardown eventually reaches this array case in `obj_free`. Because the array remains non-embedded and step 8 left its heap pointer stale, `obj_free` frees the same pointer a second time. The saved ASan crash stack shows this second free via `obj_free -> mrb_free -> mrb_default_allocf`.

cross_validation.patch_resolves_note: The patch removes the `mrb_free(mrb, p)` call from the `p2 == NULL` branch in `mrb_realloc`, so an OOM during array growth no longer frees the live element buffer before later teardown.

poc.trigger: The staged witness is the exact text `ruby_fuzzer::Function` message in `gt_results/arvo_23801/poc`. `proto_to_ruby.cpp` converts it into Ruby whose relevant fragment is `[1, (0)].insert((((1 >> ((1 - (7)) * (10))) >> 1) - (1 - ((9) >> ((1 - (11)) - (11))))))`; mruby evaluates that to the single positive index `576460752322297855` and an empty insert payload `[]`. `Array#insert` therefore executes `self[idx, 0] = []`, which makes `mrb_ary_splice` request growth to exactly `576460752322297855` elements and reach the failing `mrb_realloc` path that frees the old buffer and later double-frees it during teardown.

format.contract: Exactly the staged text witness observed in `gt_results/arvo_23801/poc`, or any equivalent `Function` message that `proto_to_ruby.cpp` converts into the same relevant Ruby fragment `[1, (0)].insert((((1 >> ((1 - (7)) * (10))) >> 1) - (1 - ((9) >> ((1 - (11)) - (11))))))`. The trigger depends on that specific arithmetic edge case producing the positive insert index `576460752322297855` with no inserted objects, so `Array#insert` grows the two-element heap array to that exact length and enters the realloc-failure path in vulnerable `mrb_realloc`.
